extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom managers, journalism educators and students
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of ethical principles, tensions, and practical standards for producing and managing journalism in digital/mixed newsrooms, including use of citizen content, social media, and digital images. Aims to guide editors and journalists in adapting traditional media ethics to an online, always-on, layered media environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should uphold the principles of accuracy and pre-publication verification even in a fast, online environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed puts pressure on newsrooms to publish before adequately checking sources and the reliability of alleged facts; major organizations too often pick up online rumors. The text gives examples (false reports of a fired coach; false reports of terrorism or nuclear meltdown) to illustrate potential harm. The criterion implies maintaining verification standards despite immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy versus gate-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between traditional gate-keeping values (accuracy, pre-publication verification, balance, impartiality) and online values (immediacy, transparency, partiality, post-publication correction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must decide how to reconcile the culture of online journalism — which emphasizes immediacy and post-publication correction — with traditional newsroom gate-keeping. The piece frames this as a foundational ethical tension for digital media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and corrections (including 'unpublishing')
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines are needed for handling errors and corrections in constantly-updated online reporting, including whether to correct publicly or remove original mistakes ('unpublishing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists increasingly blog 'live' and make errors. Questions: Should organizations go back and correct all mistakes that populate mountains of material? Or correct later and not leave a trace? The ethical challenge is to articulate guidelines consistent with accuracy, verification, and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance, impartiality, and partisan/opinion journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess when impartiality/objectivity should be preserved versus when opinionated or partisan journalism is ethically permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New media encourages candid opinion; many bloggers and online journalists identify as partisans or activists. The rubric asks whether objectivity should be abandoned, which model best serves democracy, and how to treat analysts or reporters who openly take sides. It also notes historical roots of partisan journalism and the revival of opinion-style coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and newsrooms must manage conflicts of interest and maintain independence from groups they cover and from funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some partisan journalists reject conflict-of-interest charges when they accept money or donate to parties. Entrepreneurial funding raises questions about how independent newsrooms can be and whether they will transparently report donors and conditions. Newsrooms must decide how to define independent journalism in the public interest in this context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity: when ethically permissible and platform consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine when anonymity is ethically permissible and whether rules on anonymity should be consistent across offline and online platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity is more accepted online; codes caution use of anonymous sources sparingly. Online anonymity can protect speech and expose wrongdoing but also encourage irresponsible or harmful comments. The text raises the ethical puzzle of inconsistent rules (allowing anonymity online but not in newspapers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'journalist' (normative criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A normative standard that defines who counts as a journalist based on skills and ethical commitments rather than self-identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative approach: writers should not be called journalists unless they have highly developed skills (investigative capabilities, research skills, facility with media technology, knowledge of institutions, advanced communication) and honor ethical norms (commitment to accuracy, verification, truth). People who don't meet these requirements may call themselves journalists but are not considered such from this perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered newsroom editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for how different vertical and horizontal layers of an integrated newsroom (professionals, citizen journalists, bloggers, community producers, various editors) should interact and be held accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'layered journalism' model envisions vertical layers (citizen journalists, freelancers, commentators) and different types of editors (community producers, editors handling unsolicited citizen material). Ethical questions include: by what standards will professional editors evaluate citizen contributions? What are editors' responsibilities in coordinating layers?

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for citizen journalists and citizen-supplied content
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes and editorial standards for using content supplied by citizens, including vetting, source identification, and whether citizen contributors must meet newsroom standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms must establish processes for citizen-supplied material that may be bogus or biased. Questions include: How shall sources be identified? How much vetting is necessary for different sorts of stories? Should citizen contributors be made aware of editorial standards? The broader ethical question is whether consistent norms can apply across all media platforms or whether different norms are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media use by reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for reporters' professional use of social media for sourcing and branding, and limits on personal commentary that may compromise impartial reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are encouraged to use social media to gather information and build a brand, but personal comments (e.g., a beat reporter criticizing a mayoral candidate on a blog) can undermine impartiality and create conflict with editors. The ethical challenge is to develop social media guidelines allowing exploration while drawing reasonable limits on personal commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrepreneurial not-for-profit newsroom ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical standards for journalist-run, donor-funded, or reader-funded not-for-profit newsrooms, especially concerning dependence on limited donors and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With declining commercial revenues, journalists form non-profit newsrooms and solicit donations; questions arise about how independent these outlets can be, whether they will report negatively about funders, who they will take money from, and how transparent they will be about donors and conditions. The challenge is to construct ethics for this model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of images and photo/video manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards distinguishing permissible technical changes to images (tone/color adjustments) from manipulations that change meaning or content and mislead viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence of easy capture, transmission, and manipulation raises trust concerns: who sent an image and is it authentic? Photojournalists permit minor technical adjustments but draw the line at altering meaning or content; the line can be unclear (enhancing colors extensively). Editors sometimes permit manipulation for magazine covers as 'art.' Newsrooms have fired photojournalists for fraudulent manipulation; ethics must clarify difficult cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global responsibilities versus parochial journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of journalism's responsibilities given its global impact and whether media ethics should be reformulated to guide journalism with global reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As journalism achieves global reach, ethical questions include: Should media ethics reformulate its aims and norms for global impact? What would global responsibilities look like? This criterion prompts reconceiving norms beyond parochial bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rumors and rapidly circulating information
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies for responding to rumors and rapidly spreading reports in social media and citizen channels, weighing harm from repetition against speed of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because false reports can induce panic, accidents, or worse (e.g., false terrorist or nuclear incident reports), newsrooms must decide how to treat rumors online: when to report, how to verify, and the consequences of amplifying unverified claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial consistency across platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how editorial standards (verification, impartiality, anonymity rules) should be applied consistently across different media platforms (print, broadcast, web, social).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mainstream media sometimes enforce different anonymity or verification rules across platforms (allowing anonymity online but not in print). The ethical question is whether a single set of norms can or should apply across platforms or whether platform-specific norms are inevitable.
